technical_and_design_decisions: Custom modules will be packaged as Spring Boot executable uber-jars to align with standard Spring deployment patterns and support HDFS hosting and container deployment requirements.
The native WebSocket sink will leverage the Spring WebSocket module to avoid custom protocol implementation and ensure compatibility with the existing Spring ecosystem.
All CI build and test operations will use the existing Gradle wrapper (gradlew) to ensure consistent build environments across all CI agents.
Shared dependency storage will use the existing HDFS cluster to maintain consistency with the custom module hosting infrastructure defined in user story U2.
Static code analysis and violation tracking will use the existing SonarQube instance integrated with the project's code repository to avoid introducing new tooling.
Windows-based CI integration tests will run on a dedicated Bamboo CI agent to isolate Windows-specific test environments from existing Linux CI agents.
Distributed JVM test execution will use Gradle's built-in test distribution feature to avoid requiring additional third-party test orchestration tools.
assumptions: An existing Spring-based project baseline is already in place, so development work focuses on incremental additions rather than building the core framework from scratch.
The HDFS cluster used for module hosting is already operational, has sufficient storage capacity, and is accessible from all build and deployment environments.
The existing Bamboo CI server is already installed, licensed, and has basic network connectivity to target test and deployment environments.
A SonarQube server is already integrated with the project's code repository and has existing quality gates configured.
Required service dependencies (Redis, RabbitMQ) for Windows integration tests have Windows-compatible installation packages available.
The project already includes Node.js dependencies that require caching, making npm-cache a relevant solution for CI build optimization as referenced in user story U4.
Existing custom modules follow consistent packaging and classloading patterns, so the shared dependency and classloader changes will be compatible with current module implementations.
The EC2 CI environment already has Gradle configured and has access to required test infrastructure for distributed JVM test execution.
